analysis.one_liner: Bans all new oil, gas, and coal leasing on federal lands and waters, and cancels existing Arctic offshore leases.
analysis.headline: The bill to end new federal fossil fuel leases was introduced in the House on December 18, 2024, referred to the Natural Resources Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped the Interior Department from issuing any new leases for coal, oil, gas, tar sands, or oil shale on federal land, and would have permanently barred new oil and gas drilling leases in the Arctic, Atlantic, Pacific, and Gulf of Mexico. It would also have cancelled existing offshore leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea within 60 days. Existing producing leases would have continued; only the on-ramp for new federal fossil fuel production would have closed. The bill was introduced with less than three weeks left in the two-year Congress, so it never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people on the receiving end of climate change — stronger hurricanes, wildfires, drought, and rising seas — would benefit from keeping federal fossil fuels in the ground; the bill's own findings say ending new federal leases would prevent 90 percent of the potential emissions from federal fossil fuels. Communities near federal drilling and coal sites would also see less new disturbance of public land and water. Fossil fuel companies that lease federal land and waters would lose their future supply pipeline, and states that share federal royalty revenue would lose that income.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to climate change impacts

how_it_helps.text: It would bar the Interior Department from issuing, renewing, reinstating, or extending any lease for coal, oil, tar sands, oil shale, or gas on Federal land, permanently closing the Federal onshore leasing door to new fossil fuel production.

It would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to prohibit any new oil and gas leasing in the Arctic, Atlantic, Pacific, and Gulf of Mexico, and it would cancel existing leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea within 60 days.

The bill's stated basis is climate science: its findings say about 80 percent of proven fossil fuel reserves must stay in the ground to avoid 2 degrees Celsius of warming, and that ending new Federal leases would prevent 90 percent of potential emissions from Federal fossil fuels.
It leaves narrow exceptions for an imminent national security threat and for renewals needed to avoid a material breach of an existing lease contract.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies would lose access to future federal leases, including in the Gulf of Mexico, the Arctic, and federal coal country, and some existing Arctic and Cook Inlet leaseholders would have their leases cancelled. Consumers could face some upward pressure on energy prices from reduced federal supply, and states that receive federal mineral royalties would forgo that revenue.

drawbacks.text: Halting federal coal, oil, and gas leasing would reduce domestic energy supply from Federal lands and waters, which could raise energy prices and shift some production to private or foreign sources with weaker environmental rules.

The bill cancels existing leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea within 60 days, which would likely trigger breach-of-contract and takings lawsuits from leaseholders and could cost taxpayers compensation.

Federal fossil fuel leasing generates royalty and bonus-bid revenue shared with states and the Treasury; ending it removes that income stream, which state and local budgets near extraction areas would feel.
Communities and workers whose economies depend on federal coal and oil leasing would bear the transition costs, and the bill contains no worker or community transition assistance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit would be long-term: leaving federal fossil fuels in the ground is one of the clearest ways for the U.S. government to reduce future climate emissions, since it controls the supply directly rather than subsidizing it. The main costs are real and near-term: higher prices and supply tightness in energy markets that rely on federal production, lost royalties and leasing revenue for states and the Treasury, and probable legal fights over cancelling existing Arctic and Cook Inlet leases. The bill as written does not pair the phase-out with transition aid for workers or coal-dependent communities, which an honest supporter would have to acknowledge as a serious gap. And the bill never had a realistic path: it was introduced in the final two weeks of a Congress with only Democratic cosponsors, so its design flaws were never tested or fixed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final two weeks of the Congress and sent to the Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired without a hearing or a vote when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the Keep It in the Ground Act of 2023 in the House on December 18, 2024, with six Democratic cosponsors, in the final days of the 118th Congress.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Natural Resources the same day; that was the bill's last action.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel companies that lease federal land and waters are better off: the door to future federal coal, oil, and gas leases, and to renewing dormant leases, stays open, and existing Arctic and Cook Inlet leases were not cancelled.

for.name: Rep. Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 18, 2024, to ban new federal fossil fuel leasing onshore and offshore.

for.name: Reps. Rashida Tlaib, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Salud Carbajal, Pramila Jayapal, Jesús 'Chuy' García, and James McGovern
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; the record shows no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Bruce Westerman
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled action on the bill; it received no committee activity in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 7 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and with the House under Republican control the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: The bill permanently bans new oil and gas leasing across the entire outer Continental Shelf — Arctic, Atlantic, Pacific, and Gulf of Mexico — and cancels existing leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea. Companies with portfolios built on federal offshore drilling would lose their future supply pipeline. [S2]

No new coal leases, no reoffering of expiring lease land, and no renewals of nonproducing leases on Federal land. Publicly owned coal would be effectively frozen in place for existing producers only. [S2]

industries.industry: Onshore oil, gas, tar sands, and oil shale developers
industries.note: All new Federal onshore leasing stops and nonproducing leases cannot be renewed, reinstated, or extended. Because about a quarter of U.S. oil and gas output comes from Federal lands and waters, blocking the on-ramp constrains future expansion. [S2]
By constraining future fossil supply, the bill would strengthen the economic position of renewables and electrification, though the bill contains no direct support for those industries. [S2]
